solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Split up new pet’s area (8)

indicatorNotes.new: the letters come out in a new arrangement

annotation.surface: Someone is dividing up a fresh space set aside for a pet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Split up' reads like an instruction to divide the pet's area, but it is the definition, a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a couple who split up part ways, and parting is exactly what the verb describes.

entries.clue: Run away with Penelope, leaving writer behind (5)

indicatorNotes.leaving: Penelope leaves the writer out, so PEN drops from the name
indicatorNotes.behind: what is left behind is not taken along, so it is missing from the answer

blocks.note: a pen is a writing instrument; it is removed from the front

annotation.surface: Someone runs off with a woman called Penelope, abandoning an author.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Penelope abandons a novelist lover; in the wordplay the 'writer' is just a pen, taken off the start of her name.
annotation.definitionFit: A narrower sense of running away: lovers who flee their families to marry in secret, which suits running off with Penelope.

entries.clue: Man blowing top, downing this in boozer? (3)

annotation.definitionNote: a cryptic pointer rather than a synonym: 'this' is what the man is downing in the pub

indicatorNotes.blowing top: the word loses its top letter, which in a down answer is its first

annotation.surface: An angry man in a pub loses his temper while knocking back a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blowing top' sounds like losing one's temper, but here it lops the top letter off MALE. 'This' points at the answer: what you down in a boozer, a British slang word for a pub.
annotation.definitionFit: Ale is the drink a pub-goer downs.

entries.clue: Painter supporting a couple of Charlies in African capital (5)

indicatorNotes.supporting: in a down answer, a supporter sits underneath, so RA comes after A CC

blocks.note: C is Charlie in the NATO alphabet; two of them
RA = Royal Academician, the stock painter

annotation.surface: An artist is propping up two men named Charlie somewhere in an African city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supporting' only works for a down clue: the painter is placed below the other pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the city is Ghana's seat of government, one of many capitals on the continent.

entries.clue: Detective inspector held up in incident, that’s obvious (7)

indicatorNotes.held: the event holds the detective inspector inside it
indicatorNotes.up: in a down answer, going up means reading backwards

blocks.note: an incident is an event; it goes round the outside
DI is the police rank; turned upward it reads ID

annotation.surface: A police officer delayed at the scene of an incident, and the reason is plain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Held up' reads as delayed; it is two instructions: 'held' puts DI inside, 'up' reverses it.
annotation.definitionFit: Something evident is plain to see, obvious.

entries.clue: Warning about keeping setter (4)

indicatorNotes.keeping: to keep something is to hold it, so the word for 'about' holds the setter inside it

blocks.note: on = about, as in a talk on birds
the setter refers to themself as 'me'

annotation.surface: Someone gives a caution about holding on to a dog trained to point at game.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Setter' is the crossword compiler, so ME, not the dog.
annotation.definitionFit: An omen is a sign warning of what is to come.

entries.clue: Has rector reassembled group of musicians (9)

indicatorNotes.reassembled: the letters are put together again in a new order

annotation.surface: A vicar has got the church band back together.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a vicar reforming a band; 'reassembled' acts on the letters, not the players.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description: strings, brass, woodwind and percussion players performing together under a conductor.

entries.clue: Interrogate former partner for each lucrative source (7)

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner
a = per, as in £5 a head
a mine of money or information

annotation.surface: Someone questions an ex about each of their money-spinners.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For each' is A, as in 'twice a day'.
annotation.definitionFit: To examine a witness is to question them closely.

entries.clue: Fizzy drink? It might get up your nose (4)

annotation.definition2: It might get up your nose

blocks.clueFragment: It might get up your nose

annotation.surface: Bubbles from a soft drink can go up your nose.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half seems to describe the fizz; it is really cocaine, snorted.
annotation.definitionFit: Coke is both the cola and slang for cocaine.

entries.clue: Problem interrupting Kitty’s tittle-tattle (8)

indicatorNotes.interrupting: the problem breaks into the middle of CAT

blocks.note: kitty = cat; it goes round the outside

annotation.surface: A snag cuts into someone called Kitty's gossip.
annotation.walkthrough: Kitty looks like a name (or a pool of money); it is a cat.
annotation.definitionFit: Chitchat and tittle-tattle are both idle gossip.

entries.clue: Recklessly rash peer put another way (8)

indicatorNotes.Recklessly: the letters are thrown about carelessly

annotation.surface: An impetuous lord blurts something out and has to say it differently.
annotation.walkthrough: A peer is a member of the British nobility, here just fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: The word explains itself: RE (again) plus PHRASE, saying the same thing in fresh words.

entries.clue: Try to attack (4,1,2,2)

blocks.note: first meaning: attempt something, as with a task you are unsure of
second meaning: criticise or set upon someone, a British idiom

annotation.surface: Someone attempts an assault.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Try to' reads as one phrase; split it: 'Try' is one meaning, 'attack' the other. 'Have a go at' someone is British for laying into them.
annotation.definitionFit: The phrase means both to attempt something and to lay into someone.

entries.clue: Image of suspect: European blessed with good looks (1-3)

blocks.note: fit is British slang for attractive

annotation.surface: A police likeness shows a handsome European.
annotation.walkthrough: An E-FIT is the British police's computer-built picture of a suspect; 'fit' is slang for good-looking.
annotation.definitionFit: An E-fit is a composite image of a suspect's face.

entries.clue: One departing from bar providing purchase, by the sound of it (6)

indicatorNotes.by the sound of it: we want a word that sounds like the bar, not the bar itself

blocks.note: a lever is a bar that gives purchase (grip) to shift a load; said the British way it rhymes with 'weaver'

annotation.surface: Someone leaves a pub after buying drinks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bar' and 'purchase' suggest a pub round; here purchase is mechanical grip, so the bar is a lever.
annotation.definitionFit: A leaver is someone who leaves.

entries.clue: Fear a check-up involves painful experience (7)

indicatorNotes.involves: the phrase contains the answer inside it

blocks.note: the answer starts after the F of 'Fear' and stops three letters into 'check-up'

annotation.surface: A patient dreads that a medical will hurt.
annotation.walkthrough: The medical surface fits the answer, which makes the run across three words easy to miss.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an ache in the ear is one sort of painful experience, a reading the medical surface nudges toward.

entries.clue: Roll with duck in it, or chicken? (7)

indicatorNotes.in it: the duck goes inside the roll

blocks.note: a roll (of names) is a roster; it goes round the outside
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, so O

annotation.surface: Choosing between a bread roll filled with duck and one with chicken.
annotation.walkthrough: Roll and duck both look like food; the roll is a list and the duck is zero.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the cock of the farmyard, chiefly the American name, is one kind of chicken.

entries.clue: Secure anaesthetic on time (6)

indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, A on B puts A after B

annotation.surface: Someone needs a reliable anaesthetic delivered promptly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Secure' looks like an adjective describing the anaesthetic; it is the verb, to fasten.
annotation.definitionFit: A narrower sense of securing: tying an animal to a post by a rope so it cannot wander.

entries.clue: Nameless stadium in the locality (4)

indicatorNotes.Nameless: something nameless has had its name taken away, so N, the abbreviation for name, goes

annotation.surface: A local sports ground has no name.
annotation.walkthrough: N is the standard abbreviation for name.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'in the locality' and 'in the area' both mean nearby, part of a town or district.

entries.clue: Terrified old Vera took the plunge (8)

blocks.note: to take the plunge is to get married

annotation.surface: An elderly woman, scared stiff, finally dived in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Took the plunge' looks like a dive or a risk taken in fear; it is the idiom for getting married.
annotation.definitionFit: Overawed means filled with fear or awe.

entries.clue: Some say extra-large is better (5)

indicatorNotes.Some say: what people say out loud, not what they write

blocks.note: XL is the clothing size for extra-large; spoken, the two letters make the word

annotation.surface: A claim that bigger is better.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Better' is the verb, to surpass, not the adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: to better a record is to surpass it, and surpassing others is what the answer means.

entries.clue: First lady welcoming a day’s escape (5)

indicatorNotes.welcoming: EVE takes the A and D inside

blocks.note: Eve, the first woman in Genesis; she goes round the outside

annotation.surface: A president's wife welcomes a day's break away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'First lady' is Eve, not a president's wife. The ’s is 'is', and 'escape' is a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: slipping away from pursuers or a question, dodging capture.

entries.clue: Temperature in Corsica somehow a puzzle (8)

indicatorNotes.in: T goes into the letters of CORSICA
indicatorNotes.somehow: the letters are arranged in some other way

annotation.surface: The heat on Corsica is somehow a mystery.
annotation.walkthrough: The island's letters, with T added, rearrange into the puzzle.
annotation.definitionFit: An acrostic is a word puzzle where initial letters spell a word.

entries.clue: Plans to come back for something to eat (4)

blocks.note: plans of a building or town are maps; the word is then read backwards

annotation.surface: Arrangements to return for a meal.
annotation.walkthrough: SPAM is the tinned luncheon meat.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the tinned luncheon meat is one thing you might eat, deliberately vague.

entries.clue: Spot Sue on vacation taking E (3)

indicatorNotes.on vacation: Sue is vacated, emptied of her middle letter
indicatorNotes.taking: to take something on is to add it, so the emptied name takes E onto its end

annotation.surface: Someone notices Sue on holiday taking ecstasy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' reads as on holiday; it means emptied.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: to catch sight of, notice.

entries.clue: Criminal inclination (4)

blocks.note: first meaning: corrupt or dishonest, British slang, as of a crooked copper
second meaning: a natural leaning or talent, as in an artistic one

annotation.surface: A tendency towards crime.
annotation.walkthrough: Read together they suggest a criminal tendency; split them into two meanings.
annotation.definitionFit: Bent means corrupt, and a bent is a natural inclination.

entries.clue: Happy to stand in for daughter (8)

blocks.note: to relieve a worker is to take over their shift

annotation.surface: A parent is glad to cover for their daughter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stand in for daughter' looks like a single phrase; 'for' belongs to 'stand in', and D just follows.
annotation.definitionFit: Relieved means happy that a worry has passed.
